title: Operator Review Manifest and Final-Brake Approval Doctrine
claim: FP-MCP-272 records that ForgePilot assumes competent domain operators; the approval popup is a final brake after review, not the review itself, and persistent approval is inappropriate only for fresh-scoped high-significance actions whose safety depends on current execution state.
summary: This checkpoint refines the FP-MCP-269/270/271 popup discussion. ForgePilot is not a consumer hand-holding wrapper or magical black box. It is an operator system intended for competent domain operators across fields, including but not limited to software development. No UI can prevent ignorant decisions. ForgePilot's safety responsibility is to prevent hidden scope, ambiguous authority, stale evidence, silent escalation, and unrecorded decisions, not to substitute for domain judgment. Human approval is meaningful only after the operator has reviewed the relevant packet, request, approval, artifact, workspace, commit, model, run mode, expiry, and side-effect evidence. The popup is the final confirmation boundary, analogous to a file-deletion or deploy confirmation: if the operator approves, the bounded action proceeds. Therefore, a popup is not itself the review process; it is a brake in case the AI selected or prepared the wrong action. Always allow is not universally bad and may be acceptable for stable low-risk observers, but it is forbidden by operator rule for fresh-scoped high-significance actions such as clearance creation, approval consumption, disable-switch changes, runner start, OpenCode start, prompt submission, and wait-endpoint calls, because those actions require fresh review of current state each time. Future clearance/execution workflows should present a review manifest before invoking the final popup so the operator knows exactly which files/artifacts and fields must be inspected before choosing Deny or Allow once.
caveats: This is a doctrine and requirements checkpoint, not an implementation of a new preview tool or UI override.
ForgePilot cannot make approval by an unqualified or inattentive person safe; it can only expose scope, evidence, and consequences for a competent operator.

The platform popup may still expose Always allow. FP-MCP-272 records an operator rule against using it for fresh-scoped high-significance actions; it does not prove the platform can suppress the button.
A review manifest must not become ritualized boilerplate. It must point to concrete files/artifacts/fields that the operator is responsible for checking.
This doctrine applies beyond software development: any domain-specific ForgePilot usage assumes competent operators in that domain.

doctrine.competencePrecondition: ForgePilot assumes a competent domain operator; it does not attempt to make execution safe for unqualified use.
systemResponsibility: prevent stale evidence masquerading as current authority
notSystemResponsibility: make dangerous actions safe merely by adding UI friction
turn approval popups into training or hand-holding
doctrine.fileDeletionAnalogy: The popup is like file deletion confirmation: it marks the point where the operator accepts that the bounded action will occur if approved.

persistentApprovalAllowedFor: repetitive non-mutating diagnostics whose safety does not depend on current execution tuple
persistentApprovalForbiddenFor: OpenCode HTTP session creation when coupled to execution
actions whose safety depends on current packet/request/commit/model/runMode/approval/clearance state
operatorRule.reason: Fresh-scoped high-significance actions require current operator judgment each time; persistent approval bypasses the final-brake semantics.

reviewManifestRequirement.principle: Before invoking a clearance-creating or execution-bearing popup, ForgePilot should present a concrete review manifest identifying the exact artifacts and fields the competent operator must inspect.
requiredArtifactsForClearanceApproval: target execution commit or equivalent bounded commit
requiredSideEffectFields: whether a clearance file will be written
whether disable switch will be cleared
whether runner start endpoint will be contacted
whether OpenCode HTTP session will be created
whether a prompt will be submitted
whether wait endpoint will be called
whether action is bounded to exact tuple
reviewManifestRequirement.operatorAcknowledgementModel: The operator reviews the manifest and artifacts, then treats the popup as final confirmation; Deny means stop, Allow once means proceed with the bounded action.

relationshipToPriorPackets.FP-MCP-269: Human-attention requirements remain valid but are reframed as support for competent operator review, not consumer hand-holding.
relationshipToPriorPackets.FP-MCP-270: Popup surface compliance was unresolved and required implementation or limitation handling.
relationshipToPriorPackets.FP-MCP-271: Actual clearance popup was observed and found partially informative but not compliant by itself; FP-MCP-272 clarifies that the popup is only the final brake and must be preceded by review.
relationshipToPriorPackets.FP-027: Still deferred until review-manifest or risk-exception handling is explicit enough for a guarded runner start canary.
